assumptions: That the 15:06Z deploy is related to the incident at all — this rests entirely on the three-minute gap between the deploy and the first latency warning; the contents of the revision were never examined.
That the service's behaviour returned to normal by itself. No mitigating action was taken, and no evidence was gathered explaining why the alert cleared at 15:12Z; recovery may be transient.

The 12% error figure repeated in the investigator's hypotheses is the investigator's own reading, not a measured value, and does not match the 6.5% impact recorded for the incident. Neither number was independently verified here.
That the incident was confined to io-shop. No other service was examined, so a shared dependency affecting more than one service cannot be ruled out.

That the retrieved log lines are representative. The same handful of lines was returned repeatedly across three investigation rounds, and no evidence beyond them was ever obtained, so the investigation reached its conclusion on an unchanging and very thin evidence base.
input.executive_summary: For roughly two and a half minutes on 12 September 2026, starting at 15:09 UTC, one online service became progressively slower until a share of requests exceeded the five-second timeout and failed outright. Customers making those requests would have seen slow responses or errors; the rest of traffic was served normally. The automated responder investigated for the full duration but took no action: the only cause it could name — a software release pushed to the service three minutes before the slowdown began — had no safe, reversible remedy available to it, so nothing was rolled back, restarted, or reconfigured. The service recovered on its own at 15:12 UTC and the incident was handed to a human engineer with the cause still unconfirmed. Because no fix was applied and the cause was never verified, the same failure can recur; a human should confirm or rule out the recent release and inspect the service's downstream dependencies before closing this out.
input.root_cause: Not established. The only substantive candidate is the 15:06Z deploy of revision 9f4c1e7b2a3d5c8e1f0b6a4d2c9e7b5a3f1d8c6e — the sole recorded change to io-shop in the lookback window, followed one minute later by p95 climbing from a ~220ms baseline through 900ms and 1800ms to the 5000ms request timeout — but the evidence supporting it is purely temporal: the retrieved logs contain only generic latency and timeout lines with no stack, no dependency name, no flag evaluation, and no description of what the revision changed. A slow downstream dependency or resource saturation unrelated to the deploy would produce the same latency-then-timeout shape and was never excluded. No mitigation was attempted (each proposed cause was rejected at the tier gate because no reversible action was offered), so nothing was proved by intervention either; why the incident ended is also unexplained.
